name: Tumtum

earlier_scan.note: Glottolog lists only wordlists/surveys (Meinhof 1916-17; Schadeberg 1994; MacDiarmid 1931); no grammar or phonology of Tumtum exists

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict, since no source states a stress placement for Tumtum. There is a difference of characterisation at the Kadu group level between the one work opened in full here, Schadeberg 1994 ('all Kadu languages are almost certainly tone languages', two tones + downstep, stress never mentioned), and the Google-snippet-only Stevenson 1956-57 statement already logged in 'dynamic accent (stress) plays a greater role than syllable pitch, but most languages have some lexical tone doublets'), which was illustrated from Katcha/Krongo/Kamdang rather than Tumtum. Seligmann 1910-11 (opened earlier, scanned) writes stress ticks on Tumtum forms in a wordlist without any statement of where stress falls. None of the three is Tumtum-specific on stress, and none gives a rule.

sources.citation: Seligmann, Brenda Z. 1910-11. Note on the language of the Nubas of Southern Kordofan. Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 1: 167-188.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: First published Tumtum data (Tumtum column of a seven-dialect wordlist plus sentences). Transliteration note p. 171: 'Long and short vowels are marked [macron] and [breve] respectively and stress is indicated by \'.' Stress ticks appear in the wordlist but no statement of where stress falls; no phonology section.

sources.note: 'Eastern: KRONGO, TUMTUM. Examples from KATCHA, unless otherwise stated.. Stevenson states that tone is less important than stress.. Stress is sometimes linked with tone: KRONGO.. Tone and Stress, however, are not marked in the following sections.' Second-hand from Stevenson; no placement rule; nothing Tumtum-specific.

sources.note: Group-level (Kadugli-Krongo, Eastern: Krongo, Tumtum): 'Dynamic accent (stress) plays a greater role than syllable pitch, but most languages have some lexical tone doublets.. Lexical stress-tone doublets also occur, e.g. KRONGO \'kurugu husks, ku\'rugu kidneys.' Examples from Katcha/Krongo/Kamdang only; no placement rule; nothing Tumtum-specific. Snippet reconstruction, not full text.
